chapters.title: Story of the Door
paragraphs: Mr. Utterson the lawyer was a man of rough features that never lit up with a smile—cold, sparing, and awkward in conversation; reserved in feeling; lean, long, dusty, dreary, and yet somehow lovable. At friendly gatherings, when the wine suited his taste, something deeply human shone from his eye—something that never made it into his speech, but spoke not only in the silent signs on his post-dinner face, but louder and more often in the actions of his life. He was strict with himself: he drank gin alone, to discipline his taste for fine wines; and though he enjoyed the theatre, he had not crossed the door of one in twenty years. But he extended a settled tolerance to others—sometimes wondering, almost with envy, at the wild energy that drove their misdeeds; and in any extremity he was inclined to help rather than condemn. “I lean towards Cain’s heresy,” he used to say in his quaint way (Cain being the man in Genesis who asked, “Am I my brother’s keeper?”): “I let my brother go to the devil in his own way.” In this role it was often his lot to be the last respectable acquaintance and the last good influence in the lives of men who were going down. And towards such men, as long as they came to his rooms, he never showed the slightest change in his manner.

This was no doubt easy for Mr. Utterson, since he was undemonstrative at the best of times, and even his friendships seemed founded on a similar broad good-nature. It is the mark of a modest man to accept his circle of friends ready-made from the hands of chance; and that was the lawyer’s way. His friends were either blood relations or men he had known the longest; his affections, like ivy, were the growth of time, and implied nothing special about their object. Hence, no doubt, the bond between him and Mr. Richard Enfield, his distant kinsman, the well-known man about town. What these two could see in each other, or what subject they could find in common, was a puzzle to many. People who met them on their Sunday walks reported that they said nothing, looked unusually dull, and would greet the appearance of a friend with obvious relief. Still, the two men placed the highest value on these outings, counted them the chief jewel of each week, and not only put aside chances for pleasure but even resisted business calls so they could enjoy them uninterrupted.

On one of these rambles, their walk happened to lead them down a side street in a busy quarter of London. The street was small and what people called quiet, but on weekdays it did a thriving trade. The residents all seemed to be doing well, and all were eager to do better still, spending the surplus of their earnings on display; so the shop fronts along that thoroughfare stood with an inviting air, like rows of smiling saleswomen. Even on Sunday, when the street veiled its more showy charms and lay comparatively empty of traffic, it shone out against its grimy neighbourhood like a fire in a forest; and with its freshly painted shutters, well-polished brasswork, and overall cleanliness and cheerfulness, it instantly caught and pleased the eye of any passerby.

Two doors from one corner, on the left going east, the line of buildings was broken by the entrance of a courtyard; and at that very point a sinister block of building thrust its gable forward onto the street. It was two storeys high, showed no window—nothing but a door on the lower floor and a blind, discoloured wall above—and bore in every feature the marks of long and squalid neglect. The door, which had neither bell nor knocker, was blistered and stained. Tramps slouched into the recess and struck matches on the panels; children kept shop on the steps; schoolboys had tried their knives on the mouldings; and for nearly a generation no one had appeared to drive away these random visitors or repair the damage they did.
Mr. Enfield and the lawyer were on the other side of the side street; but as they came abreast of the entry, Enfield lifted his cane and pointed.
“Did you ever notice that door?” he asked; and when his companion said yes, he added, “In my mind it’s connected with a very strange story.”
“Really?” said Mr. Utterson, with a slight change in his voice. “And what was that?”

“Well, it was like this,” Mr. Enfield said. “I was walking home from a place at the end of the world, about three o’clock on a black winter morning, and my route took me through a part of town where there was literally nothing to be seen but lamps. Street after street with everyone asleep—street after street lit up as if for a procession and as empty as a church—until at last I reached that state of mind where a man listens and listens and starts to long for the sight of a policeman. All at once I saw two figures: one a small man stumping along eastward at a brisk pace, and the other a girl of maybe eight or ten running as fast as she could down a cross street. Well, sir, the two ran into each other naturally enough at the corner; and then came the horrible part of the thing. The man trampled calmly right over the child’s body and left her screaming on the ground. It sounds like nothing to hear, but it was hellish to see. It wasn’t like a man; it was like some damned juggernaut. I shouted, took off after him, grabbed my gentleman, and brought him back to where a group had already gathered around the screaming child. He was perfectly cool and made no resistance, but he gave me one look—so ugly that it brought the sweat out on me as if I’d been running. The people who had come out were the girl’s own family; and pretty soon the doctor they had sent for arrived. Well, the child wasn’t much the worse for it—more frightened than anything, according to the doctor; and you’d think that would be the end of it. But there was one odd thing. I had taken a loathing to my gentleman the moment I saw him. So had the child’s family, naturally enough. But what struck me was the doctor’s case. He was the usual cut-and-dry apothecary—the ordinary kind of doctor of the day—of no particular age or colour, with a strong Edinburgh accent, and about as emotional as a bagpipe. Well, sir, he was like the rest of us: every time he looked at my prisoner, I saw that doctor turn sick and white with the desire to kill him. I knew what was in his mind, just as he knew what was in mine; and since killing was out of the question, we did the next best thing. We told the man we could and would make such a scandal out of this that his name would stink from one end of London to the other. If he had any friends or any credit, we said, we’d see that he lost them. And the whole time, as we were laying it on red-hot, we were keeping the women off him as best we could, because they were as wild as harpies. I never saw a circle of such hateful faces; and there was the man in the middle, with a kind of black sneering coolness—frightened too, I could see—but carrying it off, sir, really like Satan. ‘If you choose to make capital out of this accident,’ said he, ‘I am naturally helpless. No gentleman likes to make a scene,’ he said. ‘Name your figure.’ Well, we screwed him up to a hundred pounds for the child’s family; he clearly would have liked to hold out, but there was something about the lot of us that meant trouble, and at last he gave in. The next thing was to get the money; and where do you think he led us, but to that place with the door?—whipped out a key, went in, and presently came back with about ten pounds in gold and a cheque for the rest on Coutts’s bank, drawn payable to bearer and signed with a name I can’t mention—though it’s one of the points of my story—but a name at least very well known and often in print. The amount was steep; but the signature was good for more than that, if only it was genuine. I took the liberty of pointing out to my gentleman that the whole business looked fishy, and that a man does not, in real life, walk into a cellar door at four in the morning and come out with another man’s cheque for nearly a hundred pounds. But he was quite easy and sneering. ‘Set your mind at rest,’ he said, ‘I will stay with you till the banks open and cash the cheque myself.’ So we all set off—the doctor, the child’s father, our friend, and me—and spent the rest of the night in my rooms; and the next morning, after breakfast, we went in a body to the bank. I handed in the cheque myself, and said I had every reason to believe it was a forgery. Not a bit of it. The cheque was genuine.”
“Tut-tut!” said Mr. Utterson.

“I see you feel as I do,” said Mr. Enfield. “Yes, it’s a bad story. Because my man was a fellow nobody could have to do with, a really damnable man; and the person who drew the cheque is the very picture of propriety, well-known too, and (what makes it worse) one of those people who do what they call good. Blackmail, I suppose: an honest man paying through the nose for some of the wild capers of his youth. ‘Black Mail House’ is what I call the place with the door, as a result. Though even that, you know, is far from explaining everything,” he added, and with the words fell into a thoughtful silence.
From this he was recalled when Mr. Utterson asked rather suddenly, “And you don’t know whether the man who drew the cheque lives there?”
“A likely place, isn’t it?” returned Mr. Enfield. “But I happen to have noticed his address; he lives in some square or other.”
“And you never asked about the—place with the door?” said Mr. Utterson.

“No, sir; I had a kind of delicacy about it,” was the reply. “I feel very strongly about asking questions; it has too much of the day-of-judgment about it. You start a question, and it’s like starting a stone. You sit quietly on the top of a hill, and away the stone goes, starting others; and presently some bland old fellow (the last one you would have thought of) is knocked on the head in his own back garden and the family has to change their name. No, sir; I have a rule of mine: the more it looks like Queer Street—like trouble, or something shady—the less I ask.”
“A very good rule, too,” said the lawyer.

“But I’ve studied the place for myself,” Mr. Enfield went on. “It scarcely seems a house. There is no other door, and nobody goes in or out of that one but, once in a great while, the gentleman of my adventure. There are three windows looking onto the court on the first floor; none below; the windows are always shut, but they’re clean. And then there’s a chimney that’s generally smoking; so somebody must live there. And yet it’s not certain even then, because the buildings around the court are packed so tightly together that it’s hard to say where one ends and another begins.”
The pair walked on again for a while in silence; and then, “Enfield,” said Mr. Utterson, “that’s a good rule of yours.”
“Yes, I think it is,” returned Enfield.
“But for all that,” the lawyer continued, “there’s one point I want to ask. I want to ask the name of that man who walked over the child.”
“Well,” said Mr. Enfield, “I can’t see what harm it would do. It was a man by the name of Hyde.”
“Hm,” said Mr. Utterson. “What sort of man is he to look at?”

“He’s not easy to describe. There is something wrong with his appearance; something displeasing, something downright detestable. I never saw a man I disliked so much, and yet I scarcely know why. He must be deformed somewhere; he gives a strong feeling of deformity, although I couldn’t point to exactly what. He’s an extraordinary-looking man, and yet I really can’t name anything out of the way about him. No, sir; I can make nothing of it; I can’t describe him. And it isn’t for lack of memory, because I tell you I can see him this very moment.”
Mr. Utterson again walked some way in silence, obviously under the weight of consideration. “You’re sure he used a key?” he asked at last.
“My dear sir…” began Enfield, surprised out of himself.

“Yes, I know,” said Utterson. “I know it must seem strange. The fact is, if I don’t ask you the name of the other party, it’s because I already know it. You see, Richard, your tale has hit home. If you’ve been inexact on any point, you had better correct it.”

“I think you might have warned me,” returned the other with a touch of sullenness. “But I have been pedantically exact, as you call it. The fellow had a key; and what’s more, he still has it. I saw him use it not a week ago.”

Mr. Utterson sighed deeply but didn’t say a word; and presently the young man went on. “Here’s another lesson to say nothing,” he said. “I’m ashamed of my long tongue. Let’s make a bargain never to refer to this again.”
“With all my heart,” said the lawyer. “I shake hands on that, Richard.”

chapters.title: Search for Mr. Hyde
paragraphs: That evening Mr. Utterson came home to his bachelor house in a sombre mood and sat down to dinner with no appetite. It was his Sunday custom, once dinner was over, to sit close by the fire with some dry theological volume on his reading desk until the clock of the neighbouring church struck twelve, when he would go soberly and gratefully to bed. On this night, however, as soon as the tablecloth was cleared, he took up a candle and went into his business room. There he opened his safe, took from the most private part of it a document marked on the envelope as Dr. Jekyll’s Will, and sat down with a clouded brow to study its contents. The will was holographic—written entirely in Jekyll’s own hand—because Mr. Utterson—though he had taken charge of it once it was made—had refused to give the slightest help in making it. It provided that if Henry Jekyll, M.D., D.C.L., L.L.D., F.R.S., etc., should die, everything he owned would pass to his “friend and benefactor Edward Hyde.” But it went further: in case of Dr. Jekyll’s “disappearance or unexplained absence for any period exceeding three calendar months,” Edward Hyde was to step straight into his place without further delay, free of any burden beyond a few small payments to the doctor’s household. This document had long been an eyesore to the lawyer. It offended him both as a lawyer and as a man who loved the sane and conventional sides of life, and who found anything fanciful immodest. Until now it had been his ignorance of Mr. Hyde that swelled his indignation; now, by a sudden turn, it was his knowledge. It was already bad enough when the name was only a name about which he could learn nothing more. It was worse when it began to be clothed in detestable attributes; and out of the shifting, insubstantial mists that had so long baffled him, there leapt up the sudden, definite image of a fiend.
“I thought it was madness,” he said, as he put the offensive paper back in the safe, “and now I begin to fear it’s disgrace.”

With that he blew out his candle, put on a heavy overcoat, and set out towards Cavendish Square, that citadel of medicine, where his friend the great Dr. Lanyon had his house and received his many patients. “If anyone knows, it will be Lanyon,” he had thought.

The solemn butler knew him and welcomed him in. He was subjected to no waiting at all, but shown straight from the door to the dining-room, where Dr. Lanyon sat alone over his wine. This was a hearty, healthy, dapper, red-faced gentleman, with a shock of prematurely white hair and a boisterous, decided manner. At the sight of Mr. Utterson he sprang up from his chair and welcomed him with both hands. The friendliness, as was the man’s way, was somewhat theatrical to the eye, but it rested on genuine feeling. The two were old friends, old mates at school and college, both thoroughly self-respecting and respectful of each other, and—what doesn’t always follow—men who genuinely enjoyed each other’s company.
After a little rambling small talk, the lawyer led up to the subject that was so unpleasantly on his mind.
“I suppose, Lanyon,” he said, “you and I must be the two oldest friends Henry Jekyll has?”
“I wish the friends were younger,” chuckled Dr. Lanyon. “But I suppose we are. And what of that? I see little of him now.”
“Really?” said Utterson. “I thought you had a bond of common interest.”

“We had,” was the reply. “But it’s more than ten years since Henry Jekyll became too fanciful for me. He started to go wrong—wrong in mind; and though of course I keep up an interest in him for old times’ sake, as they say, I see, and have seen, devilishly little of the man. Such unscientific balderdash,” added the doctor, suddenly flushing purple, “would have estranged Damon and Pythias—the most devoted friends in legend.”

This little burst of temper was something of a relief to Mr. Utterson. “They’ve only differed on some point of science,” he thought; and being a man of no scientific passions himself (except in the matter of conveyancing—the legal work of transferring property), he even added, “It’s nothing worse than that!” He gave his friend a few seconds to recover, and then approached the question he had come to ask. “Did you ever come across a protégé of his—one Hyde?” he asked.
“Hyde?” Lanyon repeated. “No. Never heard of him. Since my time.”

That was the sum of the information the lawyer carried back with him to the great, dark bed on which he tossed and turned until the small hours of the morning began to grow large. It was a night of little ease for his toiling mind, toiling in sheer darkness and besieged by questions.

Six o’clock struck on the bells of the church so conveniently near to Mr. Utterson’s house, and still he was digging at the problem. So far it had touched him only intellectually; but now his imagination was engaged as well, or rather enslaved. As he lay tossing in the heavy darkness of the night and the curtained room, Mr. Enfield’s tale ran past his mind in a scroll of lighted pictures. He would be aware of the great field of lamps of a city at night; then of the figure of a man walking quickly; then of a child running from the doctor’s; and then these met, and that human juggernaut trampled the child and walked on, indifferent to her screams. Or else he would see a room in a wealthy house, where his friend lay asleep, dreaming and smiling at his dreams; and then the door of that room would open, the curtains of the bed would be pulled apart, the sleeper called back, and there at his side would stand a figure to whom power had been given—and at that dead hour he would have to rise and do its bidding. The figure in these two phases haunted the lawyer all night; and if he ever dozed off, it was only to see it glide more stealthily through sleeping houses, or move ever more swiftly, even dizzyingly, through wider labyrinths of lamp-lit city, and at every street corner crush a child and leave her screaming. And still the figure had no face by which he might know it; even in his dreams it had no face, or one that baffled him and melted before his eyes. And so there sprang up and grew quickly in the lawyer’s mind a singularly strong, almost excessive curiosity to see the features of the real Mr. Hyde. If he could only set eyes on him once, he thought, the mystery would lighten and perhaps roll right away, as mysteries tend to do when well examined. He might see a reason for his friend’s strange preference for Hyde—or his bondage to him, call it which you please—and even for the startling clauses of the will. At the very least it would be a face worth seeing: the face of a man without bowels of mercy—a man without pity—a face that had only to show itself to raise, in the mind of the unimpressionable Enfield, a spirit of enduring hatred.

From that time on, Mr. Utterson began to haunt the door in the side street of shops. In the morning before office hours, at noon when business was busy and time was short, at night under the face of the foggy city moon, by every light and at every hour of solitude or crowd, the lawyer was to be found at his chosen post.
“If he is Mr. Hyde,” he had thought, “I shall be Mr. Seek.”

And at last his patience was rewarded. It was a fine dry night; frost in the air; the streets as clean as a ballroom floor; the lamps, unshaken by any wind, drawing a regular pattern of light and shadow. By ten o’clock, when the shops were closed, the side street was very lonely and, in spite of the low growl of London all around, very silent. Small sounds carried far; the domestic sounds out of the houses were clearly audible on either side of the road; and the murmur of any approaching passerby preceded him for a long time. Mr. Utterson had been at his post for some minutes when he became aware of an odd light footstep drawing near. In the course of his nightly patrols he had long grown used to the quaint effect with which the footfalls of a single person, while he is still a great way off, suddenly stand out distinctly from the vast hum and clatter of the city. Yet his attention had never before been so sharply and decisively arrested; and it was with a strong, superstitious foresight of success that he withdrew into the entry of the court.

The steps drew swiftly nearer, and swelled suddenly louder as they turned the end of the street. The lawyer, looking out from the entry, could soon see what kind of man he had to deal with. He was small and very plainly dressed, and the look of him, even at that distance, somehow went strongly against the watcher’s feelings. But he made straight for the door, crossing the road to save time; and as he came, he drew a key from his pocket like someone approaching home.
Mr. Utterson stepped out and touched him on the shoulder as he passed. “Mr. Hyde, I think?”

Mr. Hyde shrank back with a hissing intake of breath. But his fear was only momentary; and though he did not look the lawyer in the face, he answered coolly enough: “That is my name. What do you want?”

“I see you’re going in,” returned the lawyer. “I am an old friend of Dr. Jekyll’s—Mr. Utterson of Gaunt Street—you must have heard of my name; and meeting you so conveniently, I thought you might let me in.”
“You won’t find Dr. Jekyll; he’s away from home,” replied Mr. Hyde, blowing in the key. And then suddenly, but still without looking up, “How did you know me?” he asked.
“For your part,” said Mr. Utterson, “will you do me a favour?”
“With pleasure,” replied the other. “What shall it be?”
“Will you let me see your face?” asked the lawyer.

Mr. Hyde appeared to hesitate, and then, as if upon some sudden thought, turned to face him with an air of defiance; and the pair stared at each other quite fixedly for a few seconds. “Now I shall know you again,” said Mr. Utterson. “It may be useful.”
“Yes,” returned Mr. Hyde, “it’s just as well we’ve met; and, à propos, you should have my address.” And he gave a number on a street in Soho.
“Good God!” thought Mr. Utterson, “can he too have been thinking of the will?” But he kept his feelings to himself and only grunted in acknowledgment of the address.
“And now,” said the other, “how did you know me?”
“By description,” was the reply.
“Whose description?”
“We have common friends,” said Mr. Utterson.
“Common friends,” echoed Mr. Hyde, a little hoarsely. “Who are they?”
“Jekyll, for instance,” said the lawyer.
“He never told you,” cried Mr. Hyde, with a flush of anger. “I didn’t think you would have lied.”
“Come,” said Mr. Utterson, “that is not fitting language.”
The other snarled aloud into a savage laugh; and the next moment, with extraordinary quickness, he had unlocked the door and disappeared into the house.

The lawyer stood awhile after Mr. Hyde had left him, the picture of unease. Then he began slowly to climb the street, pausing every step or two and putting his hand to his brow like a man in mental confusion. The problem he was debating as he walked was one of a kind that is rarely solved. Mr. Hyde was pale and dwarfish; he gave an impression of deformity without any nameable malformation; he had a displeasing smile; he had carried himself towards the lawyer with a sort of murderous mixture of timidity and boldness; and he spoke in a husky, whispering, somewhat broken voice. All these were points against him, but not all of them together could explain the hitherto unknown disgust, loathing, and fear with which Mr. Utterson regarded him. “There must be something else,” said the perplexed gentleman. “There is something more, if only I could find a name for it. God bless me, the man hardly seems human! Something troglodytic—like a cave-dweller—shall we say? Or can it be the old story of Dr. Fell—disliking a man without being able to say why? Or is it the mere radiance of a foul soul that shines through and transforms its clay shell? The last, I think; because, O my poor old Harry Jekyll, if ever I read Satan’s signature on a face, it is on the face of your new friend.”

Round the corner from the side street there was a square of old, handsome houses, now mostly fallen from their former dignity and let out in flats and chambers to all sorts of men: map-engravers, architects, shady lawyers, and agents of obscure enterprises. One house, however, second from the corner, was still occupied as a single residence; and at the door of this house, which wore a great air of wealth and comfort—though it was now plunged in darkness except for the fanlight—Mr. Utterson stopped and knocked. A well-dressed, elderly servant opened the door.
“Is Dr. Jekyll at home, Poole?” asked the lawyer.

“I will see, Mr. Utterson,” said Poole, admitting the visitor as he spoke into a large, low-ceilinged, comfortable hall paved with flagstones, warmed (in the style of a country house) by a bright open fire, and furnished with costly oak cabinets. “Will you wait here by the fire, sir? Or shall I bring you a light in the dining-room?”

“Here, thank you,” said the lawyer, and he drew near and leaned on the tall fender. This hall, where he was now left alone, was a pet favourite of his friend the doctor’s; and Utterson himself often spoke of it as the pleasantest room in London. But tonight there was a shudder in his blood; the face of Hyde sat heavy on his memory; he felt (what was rare with him) a nausea and distaste for life; and in the gloom of his spirits he seemed to read a threat in the flicker of the firelight on the polished cabinets and in the uneasy starting of the shadow on the ceiling. He was ashamed of his relief when Poole presently came back to say that Dr. Jekyll was out.
“I saw Mr. Hyde go in by the old dissecting-room door, Poole,” he said. “Is that right, when Dr. Jekyll is away from home?”
“Quite right, Mr. Utterson, sir,” replied the servant. “Mr. Hyde has a key.”
“Your master seems to place a great deal of trust in that young man, Poole,” the other resumed thoughtfully.
“Yes, sir, he does indeed,” said Poole. “We all have orders to obey him.”
“I don’t think I ever met Mr. Hyde?” asked Utterson.
“Oh, dear no, sir. He never dines here,” replied the butler. “Indeed we see very little of him on this side of the house; he mostly comes and goes by the laboratory.”
“Well, good-night, Poole.”
“Good-night, Mr. Utterson.”

And the lawyer set out homeward with a very heavy heart. “Poor Harry Jekyll,” he thought, “I fear he is in deep water! He was wild when he was young; a long while ago, to be sure; but in the law of God there is no statute of limitations. Ah, that must be it—the ghost of some old sin, the cancer of some hidden disgrace: punishment coming, pede claudo—on limping foot—years after memory has forgotten and self-love forgiven the fault.” And the lawyer, frightened by the thought, brooded for a while on his own past, groping in every corner of memory in case some jack-in-the-box of an old wrongdoing might leap to light there. His past was fairly blameless; few men could read the records of their life with less apprehension; and yet he was humbled to the dust by the many bad things he had done, and lifted up again into a sober and fearful gratitude by the many he had come so close to doing yet had avoided. And then, returning to his earlier subject, he conceived a spark of hope. “This Master Hyde, if one studied him,” he thought, “must have secrets of his own—black secrets, by the look of him; secrets compared with which poor Jekyll’s worst would be like sunshine. Things cannot continue as they are. It turns me cold to think of this creature stealing like a thief to Harry’s bedside; poor Harry, what a waking! And the danger of it; because if this Hyde suspects that the will exists, he may grow impatient to inherit. Ah, I must put my shoulder to the wheel—if Jekyll will only let me,” he added, “if Jekyll will only let me.” For once again he saw before his mind’s eye, as clear as glass, the strange clauses of the will.

chapters.title: Dr. Jekyll Was Quite at Ease
paragraphs: A fortnight later, by excellent good fortune, the doctor gave one of his pleasant dinners to some five or six old friends, all intelligent, reputable men and all judges of good wine; and Mr. Utterson so arranged things that he stayed behind after the others had left. This was nothing new—it had happened dozens of times before. Where Utterson was liked, he was liked well. Hosts loved to keep the dry lawyer a while longer, once the light-hearted and loose-tongued already had their foot on the threshold; they liked to sit a bit in his unobtrusive company, practising for solitude, sobering their minds in the man’s rich silence after the expense and strain of gaiety. Dr. Jekyll was no exception to this rule; and as he now sat on the opposite side of the fire—a large, well-built, smooth-faced man of fifty, with something faintly sly about him perhaps, but every mark of ability and kindness—you could see by his expression that he felt a sincere and warm affection for Mr. Utterson.
“I’ve been wanting to speak to you, Jekyll,” Utterson began. “You know that will of yours?”

A close observer might have noticed that the subject was unwelcome; but the doctor carried it off lightly. “My poor Utterson,” he said, “you’re unlucky to have a client like me. I never saw a man so troubled as you were by my will—except perhaps that rigid pedant Lanyon, over what he called my scientific heresies. Oh, I know he’s a good fellow—you needn’t frown—an excellent fellow, and I always mean to see more of him; but a rigid pedant all the same; an ignorant, loud-mouthed pedant. I’ve never been more disappointed in any man than in Lanyon.”
“You know I never approved of it,” Utterson went on, refusing to be drawn onto the new subject.
“My will? Yes, of course I know that,” said the doctor, a little sharply. “You’ve told me so.”
“Well, I’m telling you again,” the lawyer continued. “I’ve been learning something about young Hyde.”
The large, handsome face of Dr. Jekyll went pale to the very lips, and a darkness came around his eyes. “I don’t care to hear any more,” he said. “This is a subject I thought we’d agreed to drop.”
“What I heard was appalling,” said Utterson.

“It can’t change anything. You don’t understand my position,” the doctor replied, with a certain unevenness in his manner. “I’m painfully placed, Utterson; my position is a very strange one—a very strange one indeed. It’s one of those situations that talking can’t mend.”
“Jekyll,” said Utterson, “you know me: I’m a man who can be trusted. Tell me the whole of it in confidence, and I have no doubt I can get you out of it.”

“My good Utterson,” said the doctor, “this is very good of you—downright good of you—and I can’t find words to thank you for it. I believe you completely; I’d trust you before any man alive, yes, before myself, if I could make the choice; but truly, it isn’t what you imagine; it isn’t as bad as that; and just to set your good heart at rest, I’ll tell you one thing: the moment I choose, I can be rid of Mr. Hyde. I give you my word on that; and I thank you again and again; and I’ll just add one more word, Utterson, that I’m sure you’ll take the right way: this is a private matter, and I beg you to let it rest.”
Utterson thought a little, looking into the fire.
“I’ve no doubt you’re perfectly right,” he said at last, rising to his feet.

“Well, but since we’ve touched on this business—and for the last time, I hope,” the doctor went on, “there’s one point I’d like you to understand. I really do take a great interest in poor Hyde. I know you’ve seen him; he told me so; and I’m afraid he was rude. But I do sincerely take a great, a very great interest in that young man; and if I’m taken away, Utterson, I want you to promise me that you’ll put up with him and see that he gets what’s due to him. I think you would, if you knew everything; and it would be a weight off my mind if you’d promise.”
“I can’t pretend I’ll ever like him,” said the lawyer.
“I’m not asking that,” Jekyll pleaded, laying his hand on the other’s arm. “I’m only asking for justice; I’m only asking you to help him for my sake, when I’m no longer here.”
Utterson let out a sigh he could not hold back. “Well,” he said, “I promise.”

chapters.title: The Carew Murder Case
paragraphs: Nearly a year later, in the month of October, 18—, London was shaken by a crime of singular ferocity, made all the more notable by the high standing of the victim. The details were few and startling. A maidservant living alone in a house not far from the river had gone up to bed around eleven. Though fog rolled over the city in the small hours, the early part of the night was cloudless, and the lane her window looked onto was lit brilliantly by the full moon. It seems she had a dreamy, fanciful streak, for she sat down on her trunk, which stood right under the window, and fell into a daydream. Never, she used to say afterwards, with tears streaming down her face as she told the story—never had she felt more at peace with everyone or thought more kindly of the world. And as she sat there, she noticed an aged, handsome, white-haired gentleman drawing near along the lane, and another gentleman, a very small one, advancing to meet him, to whom at first she paid little attention. When they came within speaking distance—right beneath the maid’s window—the older man bowed and greeted the other with a very charming show of politeness. It didn’t seem as if what he was saying was especially important; in fact, from the way he pointed, it sometimes looked as though he were only asking directions; but the moon shone on his face as he spoke, and the girl was pleased to watch it, for it seemed to breathe such an innocent, old-fashioned kindness of nature—yet with something lofty in it too, as of a man with good reason to be satisfied with himself. Presently her eye wandered to the other man, and she was surprised to recognise a certain Mr. Hyde, who had once visited her master and for whom she had taken a dislike. He had a heavy cane in his hand, which he was playing with idly; but he answered not a word, and seemed to listen with badly hidden impatience. And then all at once he broke into a great blaze of anger, stamping his foot, brandishing the cane, and carrying on—as the maid described it—like a madman. The old gentleman stepped back, looking very surprised and a little hurt; and at that Mr. Hyde flew past all restraint and clubbed him to the ground. And the next moment, with ape-like fury, he was trampling his victim underfoot and raining down a storm of blows, under which the bones could be heard breaking and the body jumped on the roadway. At the horror of these sights and sounds, the maid fainted.

It was two o’clock when she came to herself and called the police. The murderer was long gone by then; but his victim lay in the middle of the lane, mangled almost beyond belief. The stick with which the crime had been done, though it was made of some rare, tough, heavy wood, had snapped in two under the force of this senseless cruelty; and one splintered half had rolled into the gutter nearby—the other, no doubt, had been carried off by the murderer. A purse and a gold watch were found on the victim, but no cards or papers except a sealed and stamped envelope, which he had probably been carrying to the post, and which bore the name and address of Mr. Utterson.

This was brought to the lawyer the next morning before he was even out of bed; and no sooner had he seen it and been told the circumstances than he set his lips grimly. “I’ll say nothing until I’ve seen the body,” he said. “This may be very serious. Be good enough to wait while I dress.” And with the same grave face he hurried through breakfast and drove to the police station where the body had been taken. As soon as he entered the cell, he nodded.
“Yes,” he said, “I recognise him. I’m sorry to say this is Sir Danvers Carew.”

“Good God, sir,” exclaimed the officer, “is it possible?” And the next moment his eyes lit up with professional ambition. “This will make a great deal of noise,” he said. “And perhaps you can help us find the man.” And he briefly described what the maid had seen, and showed him the broken stick.

Mr. Utterson had already flinched at the name of Hyde; but when the stick was laid before him, he could doubt no longer—broken and battered as it was, he recognised it as one he had himself given, many years before, to Henry Jekyll.
“Is this Mr. Hyde a small man?” he asked.
“Particularly small and particularly wicked-looking, is what the maid calls him,” said the officer.
Mr. Utterson thought for a moment; then, raising his head, “If you’ll come with me in my cab,” he said, “I think I can take you to his house.”

It was by this time about nine in the morning, and the first fog of the season. A great chocolate-coloured pall hung low over the sky, but the wind kept charging and scattering these massed vapours, so that as the cab crawled from street to street, Mr. Utterson witnessed a remarkable range of shades and degrees of twilight; for here it would be dark as the end of evening, and there a glow of rich, lurid brown, like the light of some strange fire; and here, for a moment, the fog would break apart entirely and a ragged shaft of daylight would slip in between the swirling clouds. The dismal district of Soho, glimpsed through these shifting gaps, with its muddy streets, its shabby foot traffic, and its lamps, which had never been put out or had been relit to fight off this mournful return of darkness, seemed to the lawyer’s eyes like a district of some city in a nightmare. His thoughts, besides, were of the gloomiest sort; and when he glanced at his companion in the cab, he felt something of that dread of the law and its officers which can, at times, seize even the most honest of men.

As the cab pulled up at the address given, the fog lifted a little and showed him a dingy street, a gin shop, a cheap French eating house, a shop selling penny novels and twopenny salads, many ragged children huddled in doorways, and many women of many nationalities going out, key in hand, for a morning glass of drink; and the next moment the fog settled back down over that part of town, brown as umber, and cut him off from his disreputable surroundings. This was the home of Henry Jekyll’s favourite—a man who stood to inherit a quarter of a million pounds.

An ivory-faced, silver-haired old woman opened the door. She had a wicked face, smoothed over by hypocrisy, but her manners were excellent. Yes, she said, this was Mr. Hyde’s house, but he wasn’t in; he had come home very late that night, but had gone out again within the hour; there was nothing unusual in that, his habits were very irregular, and he was often away—for instance, it had been nearly two months since she’d seen him until yesterday.

“Very well, then, we want to see his rooms,” said the lawyer; and when the woman began protesting it was impossible, “I’d better tell you who this person is,” he added. “This is Inspector Newcomen of Scotland Yard.”
A flash of ugly delight crossed the woman’s face. “Ah!” she said, “he’s in trouble! What’s he done?”
Mr. Utterson and the inspector exchanged glances. “He don’t seem a very popular man,” the inspector observed. “Now then, my good woman, just let this gentleman and me have a look around.”

In the whole extent of the house, which apart from the old woman stood otherwise empty, Mr. Hyde had used only a couple of rooms; but these were furnished with luxury and good taste. A closet was stocked with wine; the tableware was silver, the linen elegant; a good painting hung on the wall, a gift, Utterson supposed, from Henry Jekyll, who was quite the connoisseur; and the carpets were thick-piled and pleasing in colour. At that moment, however, the rooms showed every sign of having been recently and hastily ransacked; clothes lay scattered on the floor with their pockets turned inside out; locked drawers stood open; and on the hearth lay a heap of grey ash, as though a great many papers had been burned. From these embers the inspector dug out the unburned stub of a green cheque book, which had survived the fire; the other half of the stick was found behind the door; and since this confirmed his suspicions, the officer declared himself delighted. A visit to the bank, where several thousand pounds were found lying to the murderer’s credit, completed his satisfaction.

“You may depend on it, sir,” he told Mr. Utterson: “I have him in my hand. He must have lost his head, or he’d never have left the stick, and above all never have burned the cheque book. Why, money’s life itself to a man like that. We’ve nothing to do but wait for him at the bank and put out the handbills.”

This last, however, wasn’t so easy to manage; for Mr. Hyde had had few close acquaintances—even the maid’s employer had seen him only twice; his family could nowhere be traced; he had never been photographed; and the few who could describe him disagreed widely, as ordinary witnesses will. On only one point were they in agreement: the haunting sense of some indescribable deformity that the fugitive left with everyone who saw him.

chapters.title: Incident of the Letter
paragraphs: It was late in the afternoon when Mr. Utterson made his way to Dr. Jekyll’s door, where Poole let him in at once and led him down through the kitchen quarters and across a yard that had once been a garden, to the building known indifferently as the laboratory or the dissecting rooms. The doctor had bought the house from the heirs of a celebrated surgeon, and since his own interests ran more to chemistry than to anatomy, he had changed the use of the block at the bottom of the garden. This was the first time the lawyer had been received in that part of his friend’s quarters, and he eyed the dingy, windowless building with curiosity, looking around with an uneasy sense of strangeness as he crossed the operating theatre—once crowded with eager students and now standing gaunt and silent, its tables loaded with chemical apparatus, its floor littered with crates and packing straw, the light falling dimly through the grimy skylight. At the far end, a flight of stairs led up to a door covered in red baize; and through this Mr. Utterson was finally shown into the doctor’s private study. It was a large room lined with glass cabinets, furnished among other things with a full-length mirror and a desk, and looking out over the courtyard through three dusty, iron-barred windows. A fire burned in the grate; a lamp stood lit on the mantel, for even indoors the fog had begun to settle thick; and there, close by the warmth, sat Dr. Jekyll, looking deathly ill. He did not rise to greet his visitor, but held out a cold hand and welcomed him in a changed voice.
“And now,” said Mr. Utterson, as soon as Poole had left them, “you’ve heard the news?”
The doctor shuddered. “They were shouting it in the square,” he said. “I heard them from my dining room.”
“One word,” said the lawyer. “Carew was my client, but so are you, and I want to know what I’m doing. You haven’t been mad enough to hide this fellow?”

“Utterson, I swear to God,” cried the doctor, “I swear to God I will never set eyes on him again. I give you my word of honour that I’m done with him in this world. It’s all over. And in truth he doesn’t need my help; you don’t know him as I do; he’s safe, he’s quite safe; mark my words, he’ll never be heard of again.”

The lawyer listened grimly; he didn’t like his friend’s feverish manner. “You seem quite sure of him,” he said. “And for your sake, I hope you’re right. If it came to a trial, your name might come up.”

“I’m quite sure of him,” Jekyll replied. “I have grounds for certainty that I can’t share with anyone. But there’s one thing you can advise me on. I have—I’ve received a letter, and I can’t decide whether I should show it to the police. I’d like to leave it in your hands, Utterson; you’d judge wisely, I’m sure; I have such great trust in you.”
“You’re afraid, I suppose, that it might lead to his capture?” asked the lawyer.
“No,” said the other. “I can’t say I care what becomes of Hyde; I’m quite done with him. I was thinking of my own reputation, which this hateful business has rather exposed.”
Utterson mulled this over for a while; he was surprised by his friend’s selfishness, and yet relieved by it. “Well,” he said at last, “let me see the letter.”

The letter was written in an odd, upright hand and signed “Edward Hyde”; and it stated, briefly enough, that the writer’s benefactor, Dr. Jekyll, whom he had for so long so unworthily repaid for a thousand kindnesses, need feel no alarm for his safety, since he had a means of escape on which he placed complete confidence. The lawyer liked this letter well enough; it cast a better light on the friendship than he had expected, and he blamed himself for some of his past suspicions.
“Have you got the envelope?” he asked.
“I burned it,” Jekyll replied, “before I thought about what I was doing. But it bore no postmark. The note was delivered by hand.”
“Shall I keep this and sleep on it?” asked Utterson.
“I want you to judge for me entirely,” was the reply. “I’ve lost confidence in myself.”
“Well, I’ll think it over,” the lawyer answered. “And now one more thing: was it Hyde who dictated the terms in your will about that disappearance?”
The doctor seemed seized by a fit of faintness; he shut his mouth tight and nodded.
“I knew it,” said Utterson. “He meant to murder you. You had a narrow escape.”
“I’ve had something far more to the point,” the doctor answered gravely: “I’ve had a lesson—oh God, Utterson, what a lesson I’ve had!” And he covered his face for a moment with his hands.

On his way out, the lawyer stopped and had a word or two with Poole. “By the way,” he said, “there was a letter delivered today: what did the messenger look like?” But Poole was certain that nothing had come except by post, “and only circulars at that,” he added.

This news sent the visitor off with his fears renewed. Clearly the letter had come by way of the laboratory door; quite possibly, in fact, it had been written in the study; and if that were so, it had to be judged differently, and handled with more caution. The newsboys, as he walked, were shouting themselves hoarse along the footpaths: “Special edition. Shocking murder of an M.P.” That was the funeral oration for one friend and client; and he couldn’t help feeling a certain dread that the good name of another might be dragged down into the whirlpool of the scandal. It was, at the very least, a delicate decision he had to make; and self-reliant as he was by habit, he began to wish for some advice. It wasn’t to be had directly; but perhaps, he thought, it might be fished for.

Presently he sat on one side of his own hearth, with Mr. Guest, his head clerk, on the other, and midway between them, at a carefully judged distance from the fire, a bottle of a particular old wine that had lain long unexposed to the sun in the depths of his cellar. The fog still lay sleeping on the wing above the drowned city, where the lamps glimmered like gems; and through the smother of these fallen clouds, the procession of the town’s life still rolled on through its great arteries with a sound like a mighty wind. But the room was cheerful with firelight. In the bottle the acids had long since mellowed; the deep colour had softened with age, the way the hue grows richer in stained glass windows; and the glow of hot autumn afternoons on hillside vineyards was ready to be set free and to scatter the fogs of London. Little by little the lawyer’s reserve melted. There was no man from whom he kept fewer secrets than Mr. Guest, and he wasn’t always sure he kept as many as he meant to. Guest had often been sent on business to the doctor’s house; he knew Poole; he could hardly have failed to hear of Mr. Hyde’s familiarity about the place; he might draw his own conclusions—so wasn’t it just as well, then, that he should see a letter that cleared up that mystery? And all the more since Guest, being a great student and critic of handwriting, would think the step natural and obliging. The clerk, besides, was a man of sound judgment; he could hardly read so strange a document without dropping some remark, and by that remark Mr. Utterson might shape his next move.
“This is a sad business about Sir Danvers,” he said.
“Yes, sir, indeed. It’s stirred up a great deal of public feeling,” Guest replied. “The man, of course, was mad.”

“I’d like to hear your thoughts on that,” Utterson replied. “I have a document here in his handwriting; it’s strictly between us, since I hardly know what to do about it; it’s an ugly business at best. But there it is—right up your street: a murderer’s autograph.”
Guest’s eyes lit up, and he sat down at once and studied it eagerly. “No, sir,” he said, “not mad; but it’s an odd hand.”
“And by all accounts a very odd writer,” the lawyer added.
Just then the servant came in with a note.
“Is that from Dr. Jekyll, sir?” the clerk asked. “I thought I knew the writing. Anything private, Mr. Utterson?”
“Just an invitation to dinner. Why? Do you want to see it?”

“One moment. I thank you, sir”; and the clerk laid the two sheets of paper side by side and carefully compared their contents. “Thank you, sir,” he said at last, handing both back. “It’s a very interesting autograph.”
There was a pause, during which Mr. Utterson struggled with himself. “Why did you compare them, Guest?” he asked suddenly.
“Well, sir,” the clerk replied, “there’s a rather striking resemblance; the two hands are identical in many points—only slanted differently.”
“Rather odd,” said Utterson.
“It is, as you say, rather odd,” Guest replied.
“I wouldn’t mention this note, you know,” said Utterson.
“No, sir,” said the clerk. “I understand.”

But no sooner was Mr. Utterson alone that night than he locked the note away in his safe, where it stayed from that time forward. “What!” he thought. “Henry Jekyll forge a letter for a murderer!” And his blood ran cold in his veins.

chapters.title: Remarkable Incident of Doctor Lanyon
paragraphs: Time went by; a reward of thousands of pounds was offered, since the public felt Sir Danvers’s death as an injury to itself; but Mr. Hyde had vanished from the knowledge of the police as though he had never existed. A great deal of his past was dug up, and none of it was to his credit: stories emerged of the man’s cruelty—as callous as it was violent—of his vile life, his strange companions, and the hatred that seemed to have dogged his whole career; but as to where he now was, not a word. From the moment he left the house in Soho on the morning of the murder, he was simply erased; and gradually, as time passed, Mr. Utterson began to recover from the height of his alarm and to grow easier in his mind. To his way of thinking, the death of Sir Danvers was more than paid for by Mr. Hyde’s disappearance. Now that this evil influence had been lifted, a new life began for Dr. Jekyll. He came out of his seclusion, renewed his old friendships, once again became their familiar guest and host; and while he had always been known for his charitable works, he was now no less noted for his religious observance. He kept busy, spent much time outdoors, did good works; his face seemed to open and brighten, as though with an inward sense of service performed; and for more than two months the doctor knew peace.

On the 8th of January Utterson had dined at the doctor’s house with a small party; Lanyon had been there too; and their host’s face had turned from one to the other just as in the old days when the three of them had been inseparable. On the 12th, and again on the 14th, the door was shut against the lawyer. “The doctor is confined to the house,” Poole told him, “and sees no one.” On the 15th he tried once more and was again turned away; and having grown used, over the past two months, to seeing his friend nearly every day, he found this return to solitude weighing on his spirits. On the fifth night he had Guest in to dine with him; on the sixth he made his way to Dr. Lanyon’s.

There at least he was not refused admittance; but once inside, he was shocked at the change that had come over the doctor’s appearance. His face had his death sentence written on it plainly. The once ruddy man had grown pale; his flesh had wasted away; he was visibly balder and older; and yet it was not so much these marks of a swift physical decline that caught the lawyer’s attention as something in his eye and manner that seemed to speak of some deep terror in his mind. It seemed unlikely that the doctor should fear death; yet that was exactly what Utterson found himself suspecting. “Yes,” he thought; “he is a doctor, he must know his own condition and that his days are numbered; and the knowledge is more than he can bear.” And yet when Utterson remarked on how ill he looked, it was with an air of great resolve that Lanyon declared himself a doomed man.

“I have had a shock,” he said, “and I shall never recover from it. It’s a matter of weeks now. Well, life has been pleasant; I liked it; yes, sir, I used to like it. I sometimes think that if we knew everything, we should be gladder to get away.”
“Jekyll is ill too,” Utterson observed. “Have you seen him?”

But Lanyon’s face changed, and he raised a trembling hand. “I want to see or hear no more of Dr. Jekyll,” he said, in a loud, unsteady voice. “I am quite done with that person, and I beg you to spare me any mention of someone I now regard as dead.”
“Tut, tut,” said Mr. Utterson; then, after a considerable pause, “Can’t I do anything?” he asked. “We are three very old friends, Lanyon; we shall not live to make others.”
“Nothing can be done,” Lanyon answered. “Ask him yourself.”
“He will not see me,” said the lawyer.

“I am not surprised at that,” came the reply. “Someday, Utterson, after I am dead, you may perhaps come to learn the right and wrong of this. I cannot tell you now. And in the meantime, if you can sit and talk with me of other things, then for God’s sake stay and do so; but if you cannot keep off this accursed subject, then in God’s name go, for I cannot bear it.”

As soon as he got home, Utterson sat down and wrote to Jekyll, complaining of being shut out of the house and asking the cause of this unhappy break with Lanyon; the next day brought a long reply, worded in places quite movingly, and elsewhere darkly obscure in its meaning. The quarrel with Lanyon was beyond mending. “I do not blame our old friend,” Jekyll wrote, “but I share his view that we must never meet again. From now on I mean to live in the strictest seclusion; you must not be surprised, nor doubt my friendship for you, if my door is often shut even to you. You must let me go my own dark way. I have brought upon myself a punishment and a danger I cannot name. If I am the chief of sinners, I am the chief of sufferers also. I could not have believed this earth held room for suffering and terror so unmanning as this; and there is only one thing you can do, Utterson, to lighten this fate of mine, and that is to respect my silence.” Utterson was amazed; with Hyde’s dark influence withdrawn, the doctor had gone back to his old work and old friendships; only a week before, the outlook had promised a cheerful and honoured old age; and now, in a moment, friendship, peace of mind, the entire course of his life lay wrecked. So great and unlooked-for a change suggested madness; but given Lanyon’s manner and words, there had to be some deeper cause.

A week later Dr. Lanyon took to his bed, and in under a fortnight he was dead. The night after the funeral, at which he had been deeply moved, Utterson locked the door of his office and, sitting there by the light of a single melancholy candle, drew out and set before him an envelope addressed in the hand and sealed with the seal of his dead friend. “PRIVATE: for the hands of G. J. Utterson ALONE, and should he die first, to be destroyed unread”—so it was pointedly marked; and the lawyer dreaded to look at what was inside. “I have buried one friend today,” he thought: “what if this should cost me another?” Then he condemned the fear as disloyal and broke the seal. Inside was a second, sealed enclosure, marked on the cover “not to be opened till the death or disappearance of Dr. Henry Jekyll.” Utterson could hardly believe his eyes. Yes, it said disappearance; here again, just as in the mad will he had long ago returned to its author, here again were the notion of a disappearance and the name of Henry Jekyll linked together. But in the will, that notion had sprung from the sinister suggestion of the man Hyde; it had been set there with a purpose all too plain and horrible. Written in Lanyon’s own hand, what could it mean? A great curiosity seized the trustee, to disregard the prohibition and dive straight to the bottom of these mysteries; but professional honour and loyalty to his dead friend were binding obligations, and the packet went to sleep in the innermost corner of his private safe.

It is one thing to hold curiosity in check, another to conquer it altogether; and it may be doubted whether, from that day on, Utterson wished for his surviving friend’s company with quite the same eagerness. He thought of him with kindness, but his thoughts were troubled and fearful. He did go to call; but he was perhaps relieved to be turned away; perhaps, in his heart, he preferred to speak with Poole on the doorstep, surrounded by the air and sounds of the open city, rather than be admitted into that house of voluntary imprisonment and sit talking with its unreadable recluse. Poole, in fact, had no very pleasant news to give him. The doctor, it appeared, now confined himself more than ever to the study above the laboratory, where he sometimes even slept; he was low in spirits, had grown very silent, did not read; it seemed as though something weighed on his mind. Utterson grew so used to the unchanging character of these reports that he gradually visited less and less often.

chapters.title: Incident at the Window
paragraphs: It happened on a Sunday, when Mr. Utterson was out on his usual walk with Mr. Enfield, that their route took them once again through the by-street; and when they came to the door, both of them stopped to look at it.
“Well,” said Enfield, “that story is over, at least. We shall never see Mr. Hyde again.”
“I hope not,” said Utterson. “Did I ever tell you that I saw him once myself, and shared your feeling of disgust?”

“It was impossible to do one without the other,” Enfield replied. “And by the way, what a fool you must have thought me, not knowing that this was a back way into Dr. Jekyll’s! It was partly your own fault that I found it out, even when I did.”

“So you did find it out?” said Utterson. “Well, if that’s so, we may as well step into the court and take a look at the windows. To tell you the truth, I am uneasy about poor Jekyll; and even from outside, I feel as though a friend’s presence might do him good.”

The court was very cool and a little damp, and full of an early twilight, though high overhead the sky was still bright with sunset. The middle one of the three windows was half open; and sitting close beside it, taking the air with a look of boundless sadness, like some disconsolate prisoner, Utterson saw Dr. Jekyll.
“What! Jekyll! Jekyll!” he cried. “I trust you are better.”
“I am very low, Utterson,” the doctor replied drearily, “very low. It will not last long, thank God.”

“You stay indoors too much,” said the lawyer. “You ought to be out, getting your blood moving, like Mr. Enfield and me. (This is my cousin—Mr. Enfield—Dr. Jekyll.) Come now, get your hat and take a quick turn with us.”

“You are very kind,” the other sighed. “I should like to very much; but no, no, no, it is quite impossible; I dare not. But indeed, Utterson, I am very glad to see you; this is a real pleasure; I would ask you and Mr. Enfield up, but the place really is not fit.”
“Well, then,” said the lawyer good-naturedly, “the best thing we can do is stay down here and talk with you from where we are.”

“That is just what I was about to suggest,” the doctor answered with a smile. But the words were scarcely out before the smile was wiped from his face and replaced by such an expression of utter terror and despair that it froze the blood of the two men below. They caught only a glimpse of it, for the window was instantly pulled down; but that glimpse was enough, and they turned and left the court without a word. In silence, too, they made their way back through the by-street, and it was not until they had come into a nearby thoroughfare, where even on a Sunday there were still some signs of life, that Mr. Utterson finally turned and looked at his companion. Both were pale, and there was an answering horror in their eyes.
“God forgive us, God forgive us,” said Mr. Utterson.
But Mr. Enfield only nodded very seriously and walked on again in silence.

chapters.title: The Last Night
paragraphs: Mr. Utterson was sitting by his fireside one evening after dinner, when he was surprised to receive a visit from Poole.
“Bless me, Poole, what brings you here?” he cried; and then, taking a second look at him, “What ails you?” he added. “Is the doctor ill?”
“Mr. Utterson,” said the man, “there is something wrong.”
“Take a seat, and here is a glass of wine for you,” said the lawyer. “Now, take your time, and tell me plainly what you want.”

“You know the doctor’s ways, sir,” replied Poole, “and how he shuts himself away. Well, he’s shut himself in the study again, and I don’t like it, sir—may I die if I like it. Mr. Utterson, sir, I’m afraid.”
“Now, my good man,” said the lawyer, “be explicit. What are you afraid of?”
“I’ve been afraid for about a week,” returned Poole, doggedly ignoring the question, “and I can bear it no more.”

The man’s look bore out his words; his manner had changed for the worse, and except for the moment he’d first announced his fear, he had not once met the lawyer’s eyes. Even now he sat with the glass of wine untouched on his knee, staring at a corner of the floor. “I can bear it no more,” he repeated.
“Come,” said the lawyer, “I see you have some good reason, Poole; I see there is something seriously wrong. Try to tell me what it is.”
“I think there’s been foul play,” said Poole hoarsely.
“Foul play!” cried the lawyer, badly frightened and, as a result, rather inclined to be irritated. “What foul play? What does the man mean?”
“I daren’t say, sir,” was the answer; “but will you come along with me and see for yourself?”

Mr. Utterson’s only answer was to rise and get his hat and overcoat; but he noticed, with wonder, how great the relief was on the butler’s face, and perhaps with no less wonder that the wine was still untouched when he set it down to follow.

It was a wild, cold March night, the kind you’d expect for the season: a pale moon lying on her back as if the wind had tipped her over, and thin, gauzy clouds racing past. The wind made talking difficult and stung colour into their faces. It seemed, besides, to have swept the streets unusually bare of passersby, for Mr. Utterson thought he had never seen that part of London so empty. He wished it were otherwise; never in his life had he felt so sharp a wish to see and touch his fellow human beings, for however hard he fought it, a crushing sense that something terrible was coming had settled over his mind. When they reached the square, it was full of wind and dust, and the thin trees in the garden lashed themselves against the railings. Poole, who had kept a pace or two ahead the whole way, now stopped in the middle of the pavement, and despite the biting cold, took off his hat and mopped his brow with a red handkerchief. But for all the haste of his coming, this was not the sweat of exertion he wiped away—it was the moisture of some choking anguish, for his face was white and his voice, when he spoke, harsh and broken.
“Well, sir,” he said, “here we are, and God grant there be nothing wrong.”
“Amen, Poole,” said the lawyer.
At that the servant knocked in a very cautious manner; the door was opened on the chain; and a voice asked from within, “Is that you, Poole?”
“It’s all right,” said Poole. “Open the door.”

The hall, when they entered it, was brightly lit; the fire was built up high; and around the hearth all the servants, men and women, stood huddled together like a flock of sheep. At the sight of Mr. Utterson, the housemaid broke into hysterical whimpering; and the cook, crying out, “Bless God! it’s Mr. Utterson,” ran forward as if to take him in her arms.
“What, what? Are you all here?” said the lawyer peevishly. “Very irregular, very unseemly; your master would be far from pleased.”
“They’re all afraid,” said Poole.
Blank silence followed, no one protesting; only the maid raised her voice and now wept loudly.

“Hold your tongue!” Poole snapped at her, with a fierceness that betrayed his own frayed nerves; and indeed, when the girl had so suddenly raised the note of her lament, they had all started and turned towards the inner door with faces full of dread. “Now,” the butler went on, turning to the knife-boy, “bring me a candle, and let’s get this over with at once.” Then he asked Mr. Utterson to follow him, and led the way to the back garden.
“Now, sir,” he said, “come as quietly as you can. I want you to hear, and I don’t want you to be heard. And listen, sir—if he should happen to ask you in, don’t go.”

Mr. Utterson’s nerves, at this unexpected turn, gave such a jolt that he nearly lost his balance; but he gathered his courage and followed the butler into the laboratory building, through the surgical theatre with its clutter of crates and bottles, to the foot of the stairs. There Poole motioned him to stand aside and listen, while he himself set down the candle, and, with a visible effort of will, climbed the steps and knocked, somewhat unsteadily, on the red baize of the study door.
“Mr. Utterson, sir, asking to see you,” he called; and even as he said it, he signalled urgently again for the lawyer to listen.
A voice answered from within: “Tell him I cannot see anyone,” it said, in a complaining tone.

“Thank you, sir,” said Poole, with something like triumph in his voice; and taking up his candle, he led Mr. Utterson back across the yard and into the great kitchen, where the fire was out and the beetles were leaping on the floor.
“Sir,” he said, looking Mr. Utterson in the eye, “was that my master’s voice?”
“It seems much changed,” replied the lawyer, very pale, but returning look for look.

“Changed? Well, yes, I think so,” said the butler. “Have I been twenty years in this man’s house, to be fooled about his voice? No, sir—my master’s been done away with; he was done away with eight days ago, when we heard him cry out in God’s name; and who’s in there instead of him, and why it stays there, is a thing that cries out to Heaven, Mr. Utterson!”

“That’s a very strange story, Poole; it’s a wild story, my man,” said Mr. Utterson, biting his finger. “Suppose it were as you suppose—suppose Dr. Jekyll had been, well, murdered—what could make the murderer stay? That doesn’t hold up; it doesn’t stand to reason.”

“Well, Mr. Utterson, you’re a hard man to satisfy, but I’ll manage it yet,” said Poole. “All this last week—you should know—him, or it, whatever it is that lives in that study, has been crying out night and day for some kind of medicine and can’t get it to suit him. It used to be his way—the master’s, I mean—to write his orders on a sheet of paper and throw it out onto the stairs. That’s all we’ve had this week: papers, a shut door, and even his meals left there to be smuggled in when no one was looking. Well, sir, every day—yes, and two or three times some days—there have been orders and complaints, and I’ve been sent flying to every wholesale chemist in town. Every time I brought the stuff back, there’d be another paper telling me to return it because it wasn’t pure, and another order to a different firm. This drug is wanted something terrible, sir, whatever it’s for.”
“Have you any of these papers?” asked Mr. Utterson.

Poole felt in his pocket and handed over a crumpled note, which the lawyer, leaning nearer the candle, examined carefully. It read: “Dr. Jekyll presents his compliments to Messrs. Maw. He assures them that their last sample is impure and quite useless for his present purpose. In the year 18—, Dr. J. purchased a fairly large quantity from Messrs. M. He now asks them to search with the greatest care, and should any of the same quality remain, to send it to him at once. Expense is no consideration. The importance of this to Dr. J. can hardly be overstated.” So far the letter had run calmly enough, but here, with a sudden splutter of the pen, the writer’s feeling had broken loose. “For God’s sake,” he added, “find me some of the old.”
“This is a strange note,” said Mr. Utterson; and then sharply, “How is it you have it open?”
“The man at Maw’s was mighty angry, sir, and he threw it back at me like so much dirt,” returned Poole.
“This is unquestionably the doctor’s handwriting, don’t you think?” the lawyer went on.
“I thought it looked like it,” said the servant, rather sulkily; and then, in a different tone, “But what does handwriting matter?” he said. “I’ve seen him!”
“Seen him?” repeated Mr. Utterson. “Well?”

“That’s it!” said Poole. “It happened like this. I came suddenly into the theatre from the garden. It seems he’d slipped out to look for this drug or whatever it is, because the study door was open, and there he was at the far end of the room, digging among the crates. He looked up when I came in, gave a kind of cry, and bolted upstairs into the study. I saw him for only a minute, but it made the hair stand up on my head like quills. Sir, if that was my master, why was he wearing a mask? If it was my master, why did he cry out like a rat and run from me? I’ve served him long enough. And then…” The man paused and passed his hand over his face.

“These are all very strange circumstances,” said Mr. Utterson, “but I think I’m beginning to see the light. Your master, Poole, is plainly in the grip of one of those diseases that both torture and disfigure the sufferer; that would explain, for all I know, the change in his voice; it would explain the mask and his avoidance of his friends; it would explain his eagerness to find this drug, by means of which the poor soul still hopes for eventual recovery—God grant he isn’t deceived! There’s my explanation; sad enough, Poole, yes, and dreadful to think about, but it’s plain and natural, it holds together, and it spares us from any excessive alarm.”

“Sir,” said the butler, turning a sort of blotchy pale, “that thing was not my master, and that’s the truth. My master”—here he looked around and began to whisper—“is a tall, well-built man, and that one was more of a dwarf.” Utterson tried to protest. “Oh, sir,” cried Poole, “do you think I don’t know my master after twenty years? Do you think I don’t know where his head comes to on the study door, where I saw him every morning of my life? No, sir, that thing in the mask was never Dr. Jekyll—God knows what it was, but it was never Dr. Jekyll; and in my heart I believe there’s been murder done.”

“Poole,” replied the lawyer, “if you say that, it becomes my duty to make certain. Much as I want to spare your master’s feelings, much as I am puzzled by this note which seems to prove he is still alive, I shall consider it my duty to break down that door.”
“Ah, Mr. Utterson, now you’re talking!” cried the butler.
“And now comes the second question,” Utterson went on: “Who is going to do it?”
“Why, you and me, sir,” was the fearless reply.
“Well said,” returned the lawyer; “and whatever comes of it, I shall make it my business to see that you don’t lose by it.”
“There’s an axe in the theatre,” Poole continued; “and you might take the kitchen poker for yourself.”
The lawyer took that crude but heavy tool in his hand and balanced it. “Do you know, Poole,” he said, looking up, “that you and I are about to put ourselves in some danger?”
“You may well say so, sir,” returned the butler.
“Then we’d better be honest with each other,” said the other. “We both think more than we’ve said; let’s speak plainly. This masked figure you saw—did you recognise it?”

“Well, sir, it moved so fast, and the creature was so hunched over, that I could hardly swear to it,” was the answer. “But if you mean, was it Mr. Hyde?—why, yes, I think it was! You see, it was much the same size, and it had the same quick, light way of moving; and besides, who else could have got in by the laboratory door? You haven’t forgotten, sir, that at the time of the murder he still had the key with him? But that’s not all. I don’t know, Mr. Utterson, whether you ever met this Mr. Hyde?”
“Yes,” said the lawyer, “I spoke with him once.”

“Then you must know as well as the rest of us that there was something odd about that gentleman—something that gave a man a turn—I don’t rightly know how to put it, sir, except this: that it made you feel cold and thin right down to your marrow.”
“I admit I felt something of what you describe,” said Mr. Utterson.

“Just so, sir,” returned Poole. “Well, when that masked thing jumped like a monkey out from among the chemicals and darted into the study, it went down my spine like ice. Oh, I know it’s not evidence, Mr. Utterson; I’m educated enough to know that; but a man has his feelings, and I give you my word on the Bible that it was Mr. Hyde!”

“Yes, yes,” said the lawyer. “My fears point the same way. I’m afraid evil was built into that connection from the start—evil was bound to come of it. Yes, truly, I believe you; I believe poor Harry has been killed; and I believe his murderer—for what purpose, God alone can tell—is still lurking in his victim’s room. Well, let vengeance be our watchword. Call Bradshaw.”
The footman came at the summons, very pale and nervous.

“Pull yourself together, Bradshaw,” said the lawyer. “This suspense, I know, is wearing on all of you; but we mean to put an end to it now. Poole and I are going to force our way into the study. If everything is all right, my shoulders are broad enough to bear the blame. But meanwhile, in case something really is wrong, or some wrongdoer tries to escape by the back, you and the boy must go round the corner with a pair of good sticks and take your post at the laboratory door. We give you ten minutes to get to your positions.”

As Bradshaw left, the lawyer checked his watch. “And now, Poole, let us get to ours,” he said, and, tucking the poker under his arm, led the way into the yard. Clouds had banked over the moon, and it was now quite dark. The wind, which only reached that deep well of a courtyard in gusts and draughts, tossed the candlelight back and forth about their steps, until they reached the shelter of the theatre, where they sat down in silence to wait. London hummed solemnly all around them, but nearer at hand the stillness was broken only by the sound of footsteps pacing back and forth across the study floor.

“So it goes, walking all day, sir,” Poole whispered; “yes, and most of the night too. Only when a new sample comes from the chemist is there any break in it. Ah, it’s a guilty conscience that’s such an enemy to rest! Ah, sir, there’s blood shed foully in every step of it! But listen again, come closer—put your whole heart into your ears, Mr. Utterson, and tell me, is that the doctor’s foot?”

The steps fell light and strange, with a certain sway to them, slow as they went; quite different from the heavy, creaking tread of Henry Jekyll. Utterson sighed. “Is there never anything else?” he asked.
Poole nodded. “Once,” he said. “Once I heard it weeping!”
“Weeping? How do you mean?” said the lawyer, feeling a sudden chill of horror.
“Weeping like a woman, or a lost soul,” said the butler. “I came away with that on my heart, so that I could have wept myself.”

But now the ten minutes were nearly up. Poole dug the axe out from under a stack of packing straw; the candle was set on the nearest table to light their attack; and they crept forward, holding their breath, to where that patient foot was still going up and down, up and down, in the stillness of the night.

“Jekyll,” Utterson cried in a loud voice, “I demand to see you.” He paused a moment, but no reply came. “I am warning you fairly, our suspicions are aroused, and I must and will see you,” he went on; “if not by fair means, then by foul—if not with your consent, then by force!”
“Utterson,” said the voice, “for God’s sake, have mercy!”
“Ah, that’s not Jekyll’s voice—it’s Hyde’s!” cried Utterson. “Break down the door, Poole!”

Poole swung the axe over his shoulder; the blow shook the building, and the red baize door lurched against the lock and hinges. A dreadful shriek, like pure animal terror, rang out from the study. Up went the axe again, and again the panels cracked and the frame jumped; four times the blow fell, but the wood was tough and the fittings well made, and it was not until the fifth blow that the lock burst and the wreckage of the door fell inward onto the carpet.

The two men, shaken by the violence they had just done and by the silence that followed, drew back a little and looked in. There lay the study before their eyes in the quiet lamplight: a good fire glowing and crackling on the hearth, the kettle singing its thin note, a drawer or two open, papers neatly arranged on the desk, and, near the fire, things set out for tea—the quietest room, you would have said, and, but for the glass-fronted cabinets full of chemicals, the most ordinary room in London that night.

Right in the middle lay the body of a man, badly contorted and still twitching. They crept nearer on tiptoe, turned it onto its back, and saw the face of Edward Hyde. He was dressed in clothes far too large for him, clothes cut to the doctor’s size; the muscles of his face still moved as if with some trace of life, but life itself was quite gone; and by the crushed phial in his hand and the strong smell of kernels hanging in the air, Utterson knew he was looking at the body of a man who had killed himself.
“We have come too late,” he said sternly, “whether to save him or punish him. Hyde has gone to his reckoning; and all that’s left for us now is to find your master’s body.”

The greater part of the building was taken up by the theatre, which filled almost the whole ground floor and was lit from above, and by the study, which formed an upper floor at one end and looked out onto the courtyard. A corridor connected the theatre to the door on the side street, and the study was reached separately by a second flight of stairs. Besides these there were a few dark closets and a large cellar. They now searched all of it thoroughly. Each closet needed only a glance, since all were empty, and all, judging by the dust that fell from their doors, had stood unopened for a long time.
